questions.stem: When did the term Big Data emerge, and why?
options: In the 1970s, when relational databases were invented
In the early 2000s, as enterprises faced unprecedented growth in the amount, speed and diversity of information
In the 1990s, when Bill Inmon defined the data warehouse
In 2015, when cloud object storage was launched
In the 1980s, when tape drives became cheap
questions.explanation: Big Data emerged in the early 2000s as traditional databases and warehouses, reliable for structured data, could not handle the new scale, speed and variety of information.

questions.stem: Which of the three Vs of Big Data refers to the speed at which data arrives?
questions.explanation: Velocity is the speed at which data arrives, often requiring real-time or near real-time processing instead of traditional batch updates.

questions.stem: In Big Data's Variety dimension, which of the following are examples of semi-structured data?
questions.explanation: Variety covers structured data (tables), semi-structured data (JSON, XML) and unstructured data (text, images, videos, audio, logs).

questions.stem: What does the Veracity characteristic of Big Data address?
options: The physical size of storage clusters
The need to ensure trustworthiness and quality despite scale and diversity
questions.explanation: Veracity, sometimes added as a fourth V, is the need to ensure trustworthiness and quality of data despite its scale and diversity.

questions.stem: What did Hadoop and HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System) allow organisations to do?
options: Store petabytes of data across clusters of commodity hardware
Replace SQL with a graph language
questions.explanation: Hadoop and HDFS allowed organisations to store petabytes of data across clusters of commodity hardware, a key breakthrough of the Big Data era.

questions.stem: How does MapReduce process large data sets?
options: By loading everything into a single server's memory
By splitting tasks into smaller units for parallel processing and then aggregating the results
By converting data into JSON documents
By streaming records one at a time through Kafka
By indexing data in a relational table
questions.explanation: MapReduce enabled parallel processing of large data sets by splitting tasks into smaller units and aggregating the results.

questions.stem: Which NoSQL database is given as an example of a graph database?
questions.explanation: The NoSQL examples are Redis (key-value), Cassandra and HBase (columnar), MongoDB (document) and Neo4j (graph).

questions.stem: Which Big Data use case involves detecting the same card being used hundreds of kilometres apart within minutes?
questions.explanation: Fraud detection in banking uses streaming analysis of card transactions to detect anomalies in real time, such as one card being used far apart within minutes.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a streaming framework of the Big Data era that enabled real-time ingestion and analytics?
questions.explanation: Streaming frameworks such as Apache Kafka, Storm and later Spark Streaming enabled real-time ingestion and analytics; Hive and Pig are query abstractions, MongoDB a document store and HDFS a file system.

questions.stem: What happened to the Big Data vendor landscape over time?
options: Cloudera and Hortonworks merged, MapR was acquired by Hitachi, and Databricks and Snowflake emerged
All Hadoop vendors were acquired by Oracle
The Apache Software Foundation bought Cloudera
questions.explanation: The ecosystem consolidated: Cloudera and Hortonworks merged, MapR was acquired by Hitachi, and newer players such as Databricks and Snowflake pushed towards unified data platforms.
